subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 1.5 Motion in Two or Three Dimensions

questions.q: Two carts move along a straight track that lies along an x-axis. Cart 1 has velocity component v_x = −8 m/s and cart 2 has v_x = +5 m/s. A student claims that cart 1 is moving more slowly than cart 2, because −8 is less than +5. Which statement correctly evaluates the claim?
options: It is right: −8 m/s is less than +5 m/s, so cart 1 is the slower of the two.
It is wrong: the minus sign gives cart 1's direction; its 8 m/s speed is greater.
It is wrong: the minus sign puts cart 1 left of the origin, and its speed is 8 m/s.
It is right: the minus sign shows that cart 1 is slowing, so it is the slower one.
optionWhy: A student who ranks velocity components as numbers on a number line picks this. Speeds are compared by magnitude: 8 m/s is greater than 5 m/s.
The sign of a velocity component shows direction only. Cart 1's speed is |−8 m/s| = 8 m/s, greater than cart 2's 5 m/s, so cart 1 is the faster cart; it moves in the −x direction.
A student who reads the sign of a velocity component as the side of the origin picks this. The minus sign gives the direction of motion; the stem says nothing about where cart 1 is.
A student who reads a negative velocity as slowing down picks this. The minus sign gives only the direction of motion; and even a slowing cart is, at this instant, moving at 8 m/s.
questions.explain: The sign of a velocity component shows direction only. Cart 1's speed is |−8 m/s| = 8 m/s, greater than cart 2's 5 m/s, so cart 1 is the faster cart; it moves in the −x direction.
questions.working: Speed = |v_x|: cart 1, 8 m/s; cart 2, 5 m/s. Cart 1 is faster and moves in the −x direction.

questions.q: The figure shows the three straight legs of a walk from Start to End; each leg's length is given in terms of a distance d. What is the magnitude of the walker's displacement from Start to End?
optionWhy: A student who treats the displacement as the distance walked picks this: d + 3d + 4d = 8d. The displacement depends only on where the walk starts and ends.
A student who ignores the direction of the westward leg, adding it as if it went east, picks this: x = d + 4d = 5d, y = 3d, magnitude √34 d ≈ 5.8d. The westward leg's x-component is −4d.
A student who finds the components −3d and 3d correctly but adds their sizes picks this: 3d + 3d = 6d. Perpendicular components combine as √(9d² + 9d²) ≈ 4.2d.
Add components (x east, y north): x = d − 4d = −3d and y = 3d. The displacement is −3dî + 3dĵ, of magnitude √(9d² + 9d²) = 3√2 d ≈ 4.2d.
questions.explain: Add components (x east, y north): x = d − 4d = −3d and y = 3d. The displacement is −3dî + 3dĵ, of magnitude √(9d² + 9d²) = 3√2 d ≈ 4.2d.
questions.working: With x east and y north: legs dî, 3dĵ and −4dî. Sum: (d − 4d)î + 3dĵ = −3dî + 3dĵ. Magnitude √(9d² + 9d²) = 3√2 d ≈ 4.2d.

questions.q: The figure shows two displacements, A⃗ and B⃗, drawn from the same point. What is the magnitude of A⃗ + B⃗?
optionWhy: Resolve B⃗: B_x = (5.0 m)cos 53° = +3.0 m and B_y = −(5.0 m)sin 53° = −4.0 m. Adding A⃗ = +4.0 m along y gives a y-component of zero, so A⃗ + B⃗ = (3.0 m)î, of magnitude 3.0 m, less than either vector.
A student who drops the minus sign of B⃗'s downward component picks this: (3.0 m, 4.0 + 4.0 m) gives √(3.0² + 8.0²) m ≈ 8.5 m. B⃗ points below the x-axis, so its y-component is −4.0 m and cancels A⃗.
A student who uses √(A² + B²) for any two vectors picks this: √(4.0² + 5.0²) m ≈ 6.4 m. That rule holds only for perpendicular vectors; here the angle between A⃗ and B⃗ is 143°.
A student who adds the magnitudes whatever the directions picks this: 4.0 m + 5.0 m = 9.0 m. That happens only for vectors in the same direction; these largely oppose each other.
questions.explain: Resolve B⃗: B_x = (5.0 m)cos 53° = +3.0 m and B_y = −(5.0 m)sin 53° = −4.0 m. Adding A⃗ = +4.0 m along y gives a y-component of zero, so A⃗ + B⃗ = (3.0 m)î, of magnitude 3.0 m, less than either vector.

questions.q: A student claims that two displacements, each of magnitude 5 m, can add to give a total displacement of magnitude zero. Which reasoning correctly supports the claim?
options: A person can walk 5 m and back again, which makes the total distance zero.
Vector magnitudes combine by subtraction, so 5 m − 5 m gives a total of zero.
Displacements are vectors, so two of 5 m in opposite directions add to zero.
A backward step has a magnitude of −5 m, and 5 m + (−5 m) gives zero.
optionWhy: A student who treats distance and displacement as the same quantity picks this. Walking 5 m and back covers a distance of 10 m; it is the displacement, not the distance, that is zero.

A student who thinks magnitudes are always subtracted when vectors combine picks this. Two 5 m displacements in the same direction add to 10 m; the sum is zero only because the directions are opposite.
A displacement has a direction as well as a magnitude. Two displacements of 5 m pointing in opposite directions, such as 5 m east and 5 m west, add to a zero vector, so the claim is supported.

A student who thinks a magnitude can be negative picks this. Magnitudes are never negative: both displacements have magnitude 5 m, and it is their opposite directions (opposite signs of their components) that make them cancel.
questions.explain: A displacement has a direction as well as a magnitude. Two displacements of 5 m pointing in opposite directions, such as 5 m east and 5 m west, add to a zero vector, so the claim is supported.
questions.working: Displacements are vectors: 5 m east + 5 m west = (+5 m) + (−5 m) = 0. Each magnitude is 5 m; the cancellation comes from the opposite directions.

questions.q: A particle moves in the xy plane with position r⃗(t) = bt² î + ct⁴ ĵ for t ≥ 0, where b and c are positive constants. What is the particle's acceleration a⃗ at the instant t > 0 when the x- and y-components of its velocity are equal?
optionWhy: Differentiate each component: v⃗ = 2bt î + 4ct³ ĵ. The components are equal when 2bt = 4ct³, so t² = b/(2c). Differentiate again: a⃗ = 2b î + 12ct² ĵ, and at that instant 12ct² = 6b, so a⃗ = b(2î + 6ĵ).

A student who does not distinguish position from velocity sets the position components equal, bt² = ct⁴, so t² = b/c, and picks this: a⃗ = 2b î + 12ct² ĵ = b(2î + 12ĵ). The condition is on the velocity components, 2bt = 4ct³.

A student who takes velocity as position divided by time and acceleration as velocity divided by time, v⃗ = r⃗/t and a⃗ = r⃗/t², picks this: the 'velocity' components bt and ct³ are equal at t² = b/c, where r⃗/t² = b î + ct² ĵ = b(î + ĵ). Velocity and acceleration are derivatives: v⃗ = dr⃗/dt and a⃗ = dv⃗/dt.

A student who takes the velocity to be the position divided by the time, v⃗ = r⃗/t = bt î + ct³ ĵ, and then differentiates it picks this: those components are equal at t² = b/c, and d(r⃗/t)/dt = b î + 3ct² ĵ = b(î + 3ĵ). The velocity is dr⃗/dt, not r⃗/t.
questions.explain: Differentiate each component: v⃗ = 2bt î + 4ct³ ĵ. The components are equal when 2bt = 4ct³, so t² = b/(2c). Differentiate again: a⃗ = 2b î + 12ct² ĵ, and at that instant 12ct² = 6b, so a⃗ = b(2î + 6ĵ).
questions.working: v⃗ = dr⃗/dt = 2bt î + 4ct³ ĵ. v_x = v_y: 2bt = 4ct³, so t² = b/(2c). a⃗ = dv⃗/dt = 2b î + 12ct² ĵ = 2b î + 12c(b/(2c)) ĵ = 2b î + 6b ĵ = b(2î + 6ĵ). Distractors: equal position components, bt² = ct⁴ → t² = b/c → a⃗ = b(2î + 12ĵ); v⃗ = r⃗/t equal at t² = b/c, with a⃗ = r⃗/t² = b(î + ĵ) or a⃗ = d(r⃗/t)/dt = b î + 3ct² ĵ = b(î + 3ĵ). Check (b = 1, c = 1): a⃗ = 2î + 6ĵ; distractors 2î + 12ĵ, î + ĵ, î + 3ĵ.

questions.q: An object's velocity along the x-axis is known as a function of time, v_x(t), for t ≥ 0. A student claims that this function alone is enough to determine the object's position x at t = 3.0 s. Which statement correctly evaluates the claim?
options: It is right: integrating v_x(t) from t = 0 to t = 3.0 s gives the object's position at t = 3.0 s.
It is wrong: integrating v_x(t) gives x(t) only up to an added constant, so x_0 is needed.
It is wrong: x(t) is found by differentiating v_x(t), and that also needs the object's acceleration.
It is right: the position at t = 3.0 s is v_x at t = 3.0 s multiplied by the 3.0 s of motion.
optionWhy: A student who leaves out the initial condition picks this. The integral gives the displacement; the position also depends on where the object was at t = 0.
∫₀^3.0 s v_x dt gives the displacement from t = 0 to t = 3.0 s. To get the position, a known position at one instant (for example x_0 at t = 0) must be added: x = x_0 + ∫v_x dt.
A student who reverses the calculus picks this. Differentiating v_x(t) gives the acceleration; position comes from integrating v_x(t).
A student who uses x = vt with a single velocity picks this. The velocity changes with time, and the starting position is unknown, so neither the product nor v_x(t) alone gives x.
questions.explain: ∫₀^3.0 s v_x dt gives the displacement from t = 0 to t = 3.0 s. To get the position, a known position at one instant (for example x_0 at t = 0) must be added: x = x_0 + ∫v_x dt.
questions.working: x(t) = x_0 + ∫₀ᵗ v_x dt′. The integral gives only the displacement; x_0 is not determined by v_x(t).

questions.q: An object moves along the x-axis with acceleration a_x(t) = kt, where k is a positive constant. At t = 0 it is at x = 0 with velocity v_0. What is its position x(t)?
optionWhy: A student who integrates without the constant from the initial velocity picks this: v_x = kt²/2 and x = kt³/6. The object starts with velocity v_0, which adds v_0t to the position.
Integrate twice, using the initial conditions: v_x = v_0 + ∫₀ᵗ kt′ dt′ = v_0 + kt²/2, then x = 0 + ∫₀ᵗ (v_0 + kt′²/2) dt′ = v_0t + kt³/6.
A student who stops at the velocity and reports it as the position picks this. v_0 + kt²/2 is v_x(t); it must be integrated once more, and it does not even have the unit of a position.

A student who uses v = at and x = vt with a = kt picks this: v = kt·t = kt² and x = kt²·t = kt³. Those products hold only for constant quantities starting from rest; here the acceleration changes and the object starts with velocity v_0, so both steps must be integrated with initial conditions, giving v_0t + kt³/6.
questions.explain: Integrate twice, using the initial conditions: v_x = v_0 + ∫₀ᵗ kt′ dt′ = v_0 + kt²/2, then x = 0 + ∫₀ᵗ (v_0 + kt′²/2) dt′ = v_0t + kt³/6.
questions.working: v_x(t) = v_0 + ∫₀ᵗ kt′ dt′ = v_0 + kt²/2. x(t) = 0 + ∫₀ᵗ (v_0 + kt′²/2) dt′ = v_0t + kt³/6.

questions.q: The table shown gives the position x of a cart moving along a straight track at five instants. Which value is the best estimate of the cart's instantaneous velocity at t = 2.00 s?
optionWhy: A student who divides the position at t = 2.00 s by the time picks this: 8.000 m/2.00 s. Velocity is a change in position over a time interval, here a small one around t = 2.00 s.

A student who thinks any interval around t = 2.00 s will do picks this, using the widest one, 1.00 s to 3.00 s: (27.00 − 1.000) m/(2.00 s) = 13.0 m/s. The cart's velocity changes, so a wide interval gives a poor estimate.
A student who reads the position value at t = 2.00 s as the velocity picks this. 8.000 m tells where the cart is, not how fast its position is changing.

An average velocity over a very small interval around t = 2.00 s is very close to the instantaneous velocity. Using 1.99 s to 2.01 s: (8.121 m − 7.881 m)/(0.02 s) = 12.0 m/s; the one-sided 0.01 s intervals give 12.1 and 11.9 m/s, all close to 12.0 m/s.
questions.explain: An average velocity over a very small interval around t = 2.00 s is very close to the instantaneous velocity. Using 1.99 s to 2.01 s: (8.121 m − 7.881 m)/(0.02 s) = 12.0 m/s; the one-sided 0.01 s intervals give 12.1 and 11.9 m/s, all close to 12.0 m/s.
questions.working: Use a very small interval around t = 2.00 s: 1.99 s to 2.01 s gives (8.121 m − 7.881 m)/(0.02 s) = 12.0 m/s (the one-sided intervals give 12.1 and 11.9 m/s).

questions.q: The graph shows the acceleration a of a cart moving along a straight track as a function of time t. The cart starts from rest at t = 0. What is the cart's displacement from t = 0 to t = 2T?
optionWhy: A student who uses the constant-acceleration equations with the acceleration at the start, a₀, for the first interval picks this: (1/2)a₀T² plus a₀T × T = 1.50 a₀T². The acceleration falls to zero during that interval, so the cart's velocity at t = T is only a₀T/2.

A student who reads the horizontal line along the t axis as the cart being at rest picks this: only the a₀T²/3 covered before t = T is counted. Zero acceleration means constant velocity; the cart keeps moving at a₀T/2 from T to 2T.

The velocity is the running area under the a–t graph: v_x(t) = a₀(t − t²/(2T)), reaching a₀T/2 at t = T. Integrating, the cart moves a₀T²/3 by t = T. After that a = 0, so the cart keeps moving at a₀T/2 and goes a further a₀T²/2. Total (5/6)a₀T² ≈ 0.83 a₀T².

A student who multiplies the cart's greatest velocity, a₀T/2, by the whole time 2T picks this. The cart moves more slowly than a₀T/2 throughout the first interval, so its displacement is less than a₀T².
questions.explain: The velocity is the running area under the a–t graph: v_x(t) = a₀(t − t²/(2T)), reaching a₀T/2 at t = T. Integrating, the cart moves a₀T²/3 by t = T. After that a = 0, so the cart keeps moving at a₀T/2 and goes a further a₀T²/2. Total (5/6)a₀T² ≈ 0.83 a₀T².
questions.working: From the graph, a_x = a₀(1 − t/T) for 0 ≤ t ≤ T and a_x = 0 for T < t ≤ 2T. v_x(t) = ∫₀ᵗ a₀(1 − t′/T) dt′ = a₀(t − t²/(2T)), so v_x(T) = a₀T/2 (the triangle's area). x(T) = ∫₀^T a₀(t − t²/(2T)) dt = a₀(T²/2 − T²/6) = a₀T²/3. From T to 2T the velocity stays a₀T/2, adding a₀T²/2. Total Δx = a₀T²/3 + a₀T²/2 = (5/6)a₀T² ≈ 0.83 a₀T². Distractors: constant a₀ to T, (1/2)a₀T² + a₀T·T = 1.50 a₀T²; at rest after T, 0.33 a₀T²; greatest velocity a₀T/2 times 2T = 1.00 a₀T².

questions.q: Carts P and Q move in the same direction along parallel straight tracks and are side by side at t = 0. The graph shows the velocity v of each cart as a function of time t. Which statement about the carts' positions is correct?
options: At t = 4 s, cart Q is 3 m in front of cart P
At t = 4 s, cart Q is 12 m ahead of cart P
At t = 2.5 s, P and Q are side by side
At t = 4 s, cart P is 4 m ahead of cart Q
optionWhy: A student who reads the velocity graph as a position graph picks this: the heights at t = 4 s, 8 and 5, are taken as positions 8 m and 5 m. Those heights are velocities; the positions come from the areas, 16 m for Q and 20 m for P.

A student who multiplies each cart's velocity at t = 4 s by the time picks this: Q 8 × 4 = 32 m and P 5 × 4 = 20 m. Q has been slower than 8 m/s for the whole interval; its displacement is the triangle area, 16 m.

A student who thinks crossing velocity graphs means the carts are level picks this. Where the lines cross, the carts have equal velocities. By then P has gone (5)(2.5) = 12.5 m and Q only (1/2)(2.5)(5) = 6.25 m, so P is well ahead.

Each cart's displacement is the area under its graph. From 0 to 4 s, P's area is (5 m/s)(4 s) = 20 m and Q's is (1/2)(4 s)(8 m/s) = 16 m, so P is 4 m ahead at t = 4 s even though Q is now moving faster.
questions.explain: Each cart's displacement is the area under its graph. From 0 to 4 s, P's area is (5 m/s)(4 s) = 20 m and Q's is (1/2)(4 s)(8 m/s) = 16 m, so P is 4 m ahead at t = 4 s even though Q is now moving faster.
questions.working: Areas 0–4 s: P = 5 × 4 = 20 m; Q = (1/2)(4)(8) = 16 m. P is 4 m ahead at t = 4 s (Q draws level at t = 5 s). At t = 2.5 s (where the lines cross): P 12.5 m, Q 6.25 m — not side by side.

questions.q: An object moving along the x axis has velocity v_x(t) = v₀e^(−t/τ), where v₀ and τ are positive constants. What is the object's displacement from t = 0 to t = τ?
optionWhy: A student who takes the average velocity to be the mean of the initial and final velocities picks this: (v₀ + v₀/e)/2 × τ ≈ 0.68 v₀τ. That mean is the average velocity only for constant acceleration; this v_x–t graph is curved, so the area must be found by integrating.
The displacement is the integral of the velocity: Δx = ∫₀^τ v₀e^(−t/τ) dt = v₀τ[1 − e^(−1)] ≈ 0.63 v₀τ. This is the area under the v_x–t curve from 0 to τ.

A student who multiplies the initial velocity by the time picks this: v₀ × τ. The object slows down throughout the interval, so it covers less than v₀τ; the displacement is the area under the falling curve.

A student who uses x = x_0 + v_x0 t + (1/2)a_x t² with the initial acceleration, a_x(0) = −v₀/τ, picks this: v₀τ − (1/2)(v₀/τ)τ² = 0.50 v₀τ. The acceleration here changes with time, so the constant-acceleration equations do not apply.
questions.explain: The displacement is the integral of the velocity: Δx = ∫₀^τ v₀e^(−t/τ) dt = v₀τ[1 − e^(−1)] ≈ 0.63 v₀τ. This is the area under the v_x–t curve from 0 to τ.
questions.working: Δx = ∫₀^τ v₀e^(−t/τ) dt = [−v₀τ e^(−t/τ)]₀^τ = v₀τ(1 − e⁻¹) = 0.632 v₀τ ≈ 0.63 v₀τ. Distractors: v₀ × τ = 1.00 v₀τ; (v₀ + v₀e⁻¹)/2 × τ = 0.684 v₀τ; constant a = a(0) = −v₀/τ: v₀τ − (1/2)(v₀/τ)τ² = 0.50 v₀τ.

questions.q: Car B moves east along a straight road at a constant 20 m/s relative to the road. A passenger in car B measures the velocity of car A, which moves along the same road: at t = 0 it is 5.0 m/s west, and at t = 5.0 s it is 10 m/s east. A's acceleration is constant. What is car A's acceleration as measured by an observer at rest beside the road?
optionWhy: Car B moves at constant velocity, so its frame is inertial and gives the same acceleration as the roadside frame. With east positive, A's velocity changes from −5.0 to +10 m/s in 5.0 s: a = 15/5.0 = 3.0 m/s² east. (Relative to the road, A goes from 15 to 30 m/s east: the same change.)

A student who converts A's final velocity to the road frame, 30 m/s east, and divides it by the time picks this. Acceleration is the CHANGE in velocity divided by the time: A's velocity relative to the road goes from 15 to 30 m/s east, a change of 15 m/s.
A student who uses the change in speed, 10 − 5.0 = 5.0 m/s, picks this. A's velocity reverses direction in B's frame, from 5.0 m/s west to 10 m/s east, which is a change of 15 m/s east.

A student who subtracts the initial velocity measured in B's frame (5.0 m/s west) from the final velocity converted to the road frame (30 m/s east) picks this: 35/5.0. Both velocities must be in the same frame; in either frame the change is 15 m/s.
questions.explain: Car B moves at constant velocity, so its frame is inertial and gives the same acceleration as the roadside frame. With east positive, A's velocity changes from −5.0 to +10 m/s in 5.0 s: a = 15/5.0 = 3.0 m/s² east. (Relative to the road, A goes from 15 to 30 m/s east: the same change.)
questions.working: East +. In B's frame: Δv = 10 − (−5.0) = 15 m/s in 5.0 s → a = 3.0 m/s² east. B's frame is inertial (constant velocity), so the roadside observer measures the same: ground velocities 15 → 30 m/s east, Δv = 15 m/s, a = 3.0 m/s² east.

questions.q: A ball is dropped inside a train that moves along a straight, level track at constant velocity. A passenger in the train and an observer beside the track each measure the ball's acceleration as it falls, and they get the same value. Which reasoning correctly explains why their measurements agree?
options: Both observers see the ball fall straight down, so both see exactly the same motion
Acceleration is a scalar, so its value does not depend on the observer's frame at all
Their frames differ by a constant velocity, which cancels from every change in velocity
Both observers measure the same velocity for the ball at every instant of its fall
optionWhy: A student who thinks the path is the same for every observer picks this. The observer by the track sees the ball move forward with the train while it falls, along a parabola; the two observers see different paths but the same acceleration.

A student who treats acceleration as a scalar picks this. Acceleration is a vector, Δv⃗/Δt. It agrees between these observers because their frames differ by a constant velocity, not because it lacks a direction.

Each velocity the observer measures equals the passenger's value plus the train's constant velocity V⃗. In any change in velocity, V⃗ appears in both the final and initial values and cancels, so Δv⃗, and hence a⃗ = Δv⃗/Δt, is the same in both frames.

A student who thinks every observer measures the velocity measured from the ground picks this. The observer by the track measures an extra horizontal component equal to the train's velocity; only the changes in velocity, and so the accelerations, agree.
questions.explain: Each velocity the observer measures equals the passenger's value plus the train's constant velocity V⃗. In any change in velocity, V⃗ appears in both the final and initial values and cancels, so Δv⃗, and hence a⃗ = Δv⃗/Δt, is the same in both frames.
questions.working: v⃗_ground = v⃗_train frame + V⃗ with V⃗ constant: Δv⃗ is the same in both frames, so a⃗ = Δv⃗/Δt is the same. Velocities and paths differ; acceleration agrees.

questions.q: The diagram shows a boat crossing a river with a steady current. The boat is steered upstream at an angle so that it moves straight across the river, along the dashed line. How long does the boat take to cross the river?
optionWhy: A student who uses the boat's speed relative to the water as its speed across relative to the ground picks this: 60 m ÷ 5.0 m/s. Part of that 5.0 m/s is directed upstream to cancel the current, so only 4.0 m/s carries the boat across.

The boat's velocity relative to the ground is its velocity relative to the water plus the current's velocity. For the boat to move straight across, the upstream component of its 5.0 m/s must cancel the 3.0 m/s current, leaving a component across of √(5.0² − 3.0²) = 4.0 m/s. Time = 60 m ÷ 4.0 m/s = 15 s.

A student who subtracts the current's speed from the boat's speed picks this: 60 m ÷ (5.0 − 3.0) m/s. The current is perpendicular to the crossing direction, so the speeds do not simply subtract; the component across is √(5.0² − 3.0²) = 4.0 m/s.

A student who always combines two speeds as √(v₁² + v₂²) picks this: √(5.0² + 3.0²) = 5.8 m/s, giving about 10 s. The boat's velocity relative to the water is not perpendicular to the current here; it is the hypotenuse, and the speed across is 4.0 m/s.
questions.explain: The boat's velocity relative to the ground is its velocity relative to the water plus the current's velocity. For the boat to move straight across, the upstream component of its 5.0 m/s must cancel the 3.0 m/s current, leaving a component across of √(5.0² − 3.0²) = 4.0 m/s. Time = 60 m ÷ 4.0 m/s = 15 s.
questions.working: v⃗_ground = v⃗_rel water + v⃗_current. Moving straight across: upstream component of v_rel cancels the current, 3.0 m/s; cross component = √(5.0² − 3.0²) = 4.0 m/s. t = 60 m ÷ 4.0 m/s = 15 s.

A dashed line runs straight across the river from the boat to the opposite bank.

questions.q: A ball is thrown from the top of a vertical cliff 25 m above the sea, with speed 20 m/s at 37° above the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.60, cos 37° = 0.80). Air resistance is negligible. Use g = 10 m/s². How long after it is thrown does the ball reach the sea?
optionWhy: A student who uses the launch speed, 20 m/s, as the initial vertical velocity picks this: −25 = 20t − 5t² gives t = 5.0 s. Only the vertical component, 20 sin 37° = 12 m/s, belongs in the vertical equation.

A student who takes the vertical component as 20 cos 37° = 16 m/s picks this: −25 = 16t − 5t² gives t ≈ 4.3 s. The angle is measured from the horizontal, so the vertical component is 20 sin 37° = 12 m/s.

A student who treats the throw like a horizontal launch, with zero initial vertical velocity, picks this: 25 = 5t² gives t ≈ 2.2 s. The ball starts with 12 m/s upward, so it first rises and takes longer to reach the sea.
Only the vertical motion sets the time. With up positive, v_y0 = (20 m/s)(0.60) = 12 m/s and the sea is at y = −25 m: −25 = 12t − 5t². The positive root is t = [12 + √(144 + 500)]/10 ≈ 3.7 s.
questions.explain: Only the vertical motion sets the time. With up positive, v_y0 = (20 m/s)(0.60) = 12 m/s and the sea is at y = −25 m: −25 = 12t − 5t². The positive root is t = [12 + √(144 + 500)]/10 ≈ 3.7 s.

questions.q: The diagram shows the paths of three balls, A, B and C, launched from the origin on level ground, and the horizontal component v_x of each ball's velocity. Air resistance is negligible. Which ranks the times the balls spend in the air, from longest to shortest?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the ball that lands farthest away must have been in the air longest picks this, ranking by landing distance. B goes farthest because of its larger horizontal velocity, not because it is in the air longer; A, with the highest arc, stays up longest.

A student who thinks a larger horizontal velocity holds a ball up picks this, ranking by v_x. The horizontal motion has no effect on the vertical motion; the time in the air is set by how high each ball rises.

The time in the air depends only on the vertical motion. A ball that rises higher had a larger upward velocity component and takes longer to rise and to fall back: A (about 11 m) stays up longest, then B (5 m), then C (about 1 m). The horizontal components do not affect the times.

A student who thinks all projectiles launched from the same height land together picks this. That is true only for equal initial vertical velocities; these balls rise to different heights, so they have different vertical velocities and different times in the air.
questions.explain: The time in the air depends only on the vertical motion. A ball that rises higher had a larger upward velocity component and takes longer to rise and to fall back: A (about 11 m) stays up longest, then B (5 m), then C (about 1 m). The horizontal components do not affect the times.
questions.working: Time of flight from vertical motion only: H = v_y0²/(2g), T = 2v_y0/g. A rises highest (≈11 m: T = 3.0 s), B 5 m (2.0 s), C ≈1 m (1.0 s). A > B > C. (Ranges: B 28 > C 20 > A 18 m; v_x: C > B > A.)

figure.alt: Graph of the paths of three balls in a vertical plane, with x (m) on the horizontal axis marked 10, 20 and 30 and y (m) on the vertical axis marked 5 and 10. All three paths start at the origin O on level ground. Path A (blue) rises highest, to about 11 m, and lands at x = 18 m. Path B (red) rises to 5 m and lands farthest, at x = 28 m. Path C (plain line) is a low arc rising to about 1 m and lands at x = 20 m. A key at the top right gives the horizontal component of each ball's velocity: A: v_x = 6 m/s; B: v_x = 14 m/s; C: v_x = 20 m/s.

questions.q: At t = 0, a particle at the origin of the xy plane is moving with speed v₀ in a direction 37° above the +x axis (sin 37° = 0.60, cos 37° = 0.80). For t ≥ 0, its acceleration is a⃗ = −kt ĵ, where k is a positive constant. At what time t > 0 does the particle return to the x-axis?
optionWhy: A student who takes the y-component of the initial velocity as v₀ cos 37° = 0.80v₀ picks this: 0.80v₀t = kt³/6 gives t = √4.8 √(v₀/k) ≈ 2.2√(v₀/k). The 37° angle is measured from the x-axis, so the y-component is v₀ sin 37°.

The y-motion is independent of the x-motion. With v_y0 = v₀ sin 37° = 0.60v₀ and a_y = −kt, integrating twice gives y = 0.60v₀t − kt³/6. Setting y = 0 gives t² = 3.6v₀/k, so t = √3.6 √(v₀/k) ≈ 1.9√(v₀/k).

A student who uses the speed v₀ as the initial y-velocity, without resolving it, picks this: v₀t = kt³/6 gives t = √6 √(v₀/k) ≈ 2.4√(v₀/k). Only the component v₀ sin 37° = 0.60v₀ is in the y-direction.

A student who uses y = v_y0 t + (1/2)a_y t² with the acceleration at the end, a_y = −kt, picks this: 0.60v₀t = (1/2)(kt)t² gives t = √1.2 √(v₀/k) ≈ 1.1√(v₀/k). That equation holds only for constant acceleration; here a_y changes with time, so v_y and y must be found by integration.
questions.explain: The y-motion is independent of the x-motion. With v_y0 = v₀ sin 37° = 0.60v₀ and a_y = −kt, integrating twice gives y = 0.60v₀t − kt³/6. Setting y = 0 gives t² = 3.6v₀/k, so t = √3.6 √(v₀/k) ≈ 1.9√(v₀/k).
questions.working: Only the y-motion matters. v_y0 = v₀ sin 37° = 0.60v₀. v_y(t) = 0.60v₀ − ∫₀ᵗ kt′ dt′ = 0.60v₀ − kt²/2. y(t) = ∫₀ᵗ v_y dt′ = 0.60v₀t − kt³/6. y = 0 with t > 0: t² = 3.6v₀/k, t = √3.6 √(v₀/k) ≈ 1.9√(v₀/k). (x = 0.80v₀t does not affect when y = 0.) Distractors: v_y0 = 0.80v₀ → √4.8 ≈ 2.2; v_y0 = v₀ → √6 ≈ 2.4; y = 0.60v₀t − (1/2)(kt)t² → √1.2 ≈ 1.1.

questions.q: A block of mass m slides onto a rough horizontal patch with speed v₀. On the patch, the coefficient of kinetic friction increases with the distance x the block has moved into the patch as μ_k = bx, where b is a positive constant. Air resistance is negligible, and g is the magnitude of the gravitational field. How far into the patch does the block slide before it stops?
optionWhy: The friction force is μ_k mg = bmgx, so its work over the slide is −∫₀ᴰ bmgx dx = −bmgD²/2. By the work–energy theorem this equals the change in kinetic energy, −(1/2)mv₀², so D² = v₀²/(bg) and D = v₀/√(bg).

A student who multiplies the friction force at the end of the slide, bmgD, by the whole distance D picks this: bmgD² = (1/2)mv₀². The force grows from zero, so its work is the integral of the force over the path, bmgD²/2, half as much.
A student who writes the block’s kinetic energy as mv₀², leaving out the ½, picks this: bmgD²/2 = mv₀² gives D = v₀√(2/(bg)). The block’s initial kinetic energy is (1/2)mv₀².
A student who takes kinetic energy to be proportional to speed rather than to its square picks this: bmgD²/2 = (1/2)mv₀ gives D = √(v₀/(bg)), which does not even have the units of length.
questions.explain: The friction force is μ_k mg = bmgx, so its work over the slide is −∫₀ᴰ bmgx dx = −bmgD²/2. By the work–energy theorem this equals the change in kinetic energy, −(1/2)mv₀², so D² = v₀²/(bg) and D = v₀/√(bg).
questions.working: F_N = mg on the level patch, so the friction force has magnitude μ_k mg = bmgx, opposite the motion. Work done by friction over the slide: W_f = ∫₀ᴰ (−bmgx) dx = −bmgD²/2. Work–energy theorem (friction is the only force with a component along the motion): W_f = ΔK = 0 − (1/2)mv₀², so bmgD²/2 = (1/2)mv₀² and D = v₀/√(bg) (sympy-checked; b in 1/m, so D is in m). Distractors: friction at the end of the slide times D, bmgD² = (1/2)mv₀², D = v₀/√(2bg); K written as mv₀², bmgD²/2 = mv₀², D = v₀√(2/(bg)); K taken as proportional to v₀, bmgD²/2 = (1/2)mv₀, D = √(v₀/(bg)).

questions.q: An object of mass m starts from rest at x = 0. The graph shows the only force with a component along its motion, F, as a function of position x. The object’s speed at x = 4x₀ can be written as v = k√(F₀x₀/m). What is the value of k?
optionWhy: A student who adds the area below the axis as positive work picks this: total 2.5F₀x₀, v = √5 √(F₀x₀/m). The force is opposite to the motion between 3x₀ and 4x₀, so that area is negative work.

A student who uses the largest force, F₀, as if it were exerted over the whole 4x₀ picks this: W = 4F₀x₀, v = √8 √(F₀x₀/m). The work is the area under the graph, not the peak force times the displacement.
A student who writes the kinetic energy as mv² picks this: mv² = 1.5F₀x₀, v = √1.5 √(F₀x₀/m). With K = (1/2)mv² the speed is √2 times larger.

The work is the signed area under the graph: (1/2)F₀x₀ from 0 to x₀, F₀x₀ from x₀ to 2x₀, +(1/2)F₀x₀ from 2x₀ to 3x₀ and −(1/2)F₀x₀ from 3x₀ to 4x₀, a total of (3/2)F₀x₀. (1/2)mv² = (3/2)F₀x₀ gives v = √3 √(F₀x₀/m) = 1.73√(F₀x₀/m).
questions.explain: The work is the signed area under the graph: (1/2)F₀x₀ from 0 to x₀, F₀x₀ from x₀ to 2x₀, +(1/2)F₀x₀ from 2x₀ to 3x₀ and −(1/2)F₀x₀ from 3x₀ to 4x₀, a total of (3/2)F₀x₀. (1/2)mv² = (3/2)F₀x₀ gives v = √3 √(F₀x₀/m) = 1.73√(F₀x₀/m).
questions.working: Areas: ½F₀x₀ + F₀x₀ + ½F₀x₀ − ½F₀x₀ = 1.5F₀x₀ = W_net = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(3F₀x₀/m) = 1.732√(F₀x₀/m) (sympy-checked). Distractors: magnitudes 2.5 → √5 = 2.24; F₀ × 4x₀ → √8 = 2.83; no ½ → √1.5 = 1.22.

The graph is a straight line rising from F = 0 at x = 0 to F = F₀ at x = x₀, a horizontal line at F₀ from x₀ to 2x₀, then a straight line falling from F₀ at 2x₀ through zero at 3x₀ to −F₀ at 4x₀.

questions.q: The graph shows the component F of the net force on an object along its direction of motion, as a function of the object’s position x. W₁, W₂ and W₃ are the work done by this force in the intervals marked 1, 2 and 3. Which ranking is correct?
optionWhy: A student who adds areas without signs picks this: 6 J, 1.5 J + 1.5 J = 3 J and 3 J. Area below the axis is negative work, so W₂ = 0 and W₃ = −3 J.
A student who ranks the intervals by the slope of the graph picks this: +1.5 N/m, 0 and −3 N/m. The slope tells how quickly the force changes, not the work it does.

The work in each interval is the signed area between the graph and the x-axis. Interval 1: (3 N)(2 m) = +6 J. Interval 2: the line falls from 3 N to −3 N, so equal triangles above and below the axis cancel: 0 J. Interval 3: the triangle from −3 N to 0 lies below the axis: −3 J. So W₁ > W₂ > W₃.

A student who ranks by the value of the force at the end of each interval picks this: 3 N, 0 and −3 N for intervals 1, 3 and 2. The work is the area under the graph over the interval, not its height at one point.
